checkpoints: Artifact identity: CI builds exactly once per commit, packages it as an immutable artifact tagged by the commit SHA (never "latest"), and transfers it to a versioned directory on the VPS (releases/<sha>), keeping the last N.

Rollback needs no rebuild: because releases are versioned and retained on disk under releases/<sha>, rollback is a single command that re-points the "currently running" pointer back to a previously retained SHA and reloads gracefully following the same process-replacement procedure — no rebuild, no dependency on an external network.

Zero-downtime process replacement: the new process starts first and the deploy waits for it to return 200 on a concrete health endpoint (GET /health) before shifting traffic, only then draining in-flight requests and stopping the old process — the opposite of kill-then-start.
Failed health check aborts the switch: if the new process never passes its health check, the switch must abort and the old process keeps serving — never shift traffic anyway.

Reverse proxy scope and independence: nginx's only job is TLS termination and forwarding to one fixed local upstream — an app release never touches nginx config/certs, and Certbot's own renewal schedule is fully independent of the app's deploy lifecycle, with nginx just reloading to pick up a new cert.
Secret boundary: the SSH key CI uses to log into the VPS lives only in CI's own secret store, injected into the deploy job at run time — never in code or on an engineer's laptop.
Audit trail: every deploy is a pipeline run with a log/audit trail (who, which commit), eliminating the risk that only one person knows how to SSH deploy manually.
Non-blocking evaluate: the evaluate(flagKey, context) call reads only the in-memory cache and never blocks on or calls the network on the request path.

Background cache refresh: a background poller runs on its own interval (independent of any request) pulling the latest flag definitions into that in-memory cache, so the non-blocking read stays reasonably fresh.

Stable hash for bucketing: bucketing hashes the user id with a hash function that is stable across processes and deploys (not a language's default/randomized hash) modulo the rollout percentage, so the same user lands in the same variant every time.
Hashing algorithm is versioned: the hash algorithm/version is itself part of the flag's config, so changing it later is a deliberate migration, not a silent re-bucketing of already-assigned users.

Cache fallback on unreachable source: when the flag source can't be reached, evaluation keeps serving the last-known cached definitions instead of erroring or forcing every flag to a single fallback value.

Per-flag fail-safe default: the safe default returned when a flag has no cached value is decided per flag by type/purpose (e.g. a release flag defaults to off/old behavior, a kill-switch may default the opposite way) — not one global fail-open/fail-closed rule for all flags.
Flag lifecycle metadata: each flag carries metadata such as type, owner, and expiry, so tooling/CI can flag stale or orphaned flags that should be removed.
Exposure logging: each evaluation records the flag key, user context, and outcome so a flag's effect can be diagnosed after the fact.
Initial hardening: create a non-root deploy user and open only firewall ports 22/80/443.
Reverse proxy install and DNS pointing: install the reverse proxy and point the domain's A-record at the VPS's IP.
Local forwarding configuration: configure the reverse proxy to forward 80/443 traffic to the app's local port.

Certificate issuance: run the cert tool, which passes the HTTP-01 challenge on its own (requiring DNS already resolving correctly and port 80 open), and patches the reverse-proxy config with the cert paths plus an HTTP→HTTPS redirect.
End-to-end HTTPS verification: confirm with curl https://domain that HTTPS actually works.
Renewal timer confirmation: separately confirm the renewal timer is active via a dry-run test, without forcing a real renewal.

Automatic renewal mechanism: renewal fires automatically once fewer than roughly 30 days remain of the certificate's 90-day lifetime, and when it fires the reverse proxy just reloads — the app is never restarted.

Issuance edge cases: DNS that hasn't propagated yet makes the issuance step fail outright, so DNS resolution must be verified first; and because the certificate authority rate-limits issuance per week, every test of the flow should use staging mode instead of forcing repeated real renewals.
Step 1 — Expand schema: ADD COLUMN role nullable, a database migration that is metadata-only and takes almost no lock.

Step 2 — Dual-write code release: deploy application code where every write path sets both the old representation and the new role column, so both old and new code versions still read correctly afterward.
Step 3 — Backfill: backfill the 12 million existing rows in small batches (a migration or background job, not one giant UPDATE) so no single lock runs long.

Step 4 — Enforce NOT NULL: ALTER COLUMN role SET NOT NULL, a migration that is cheap because the backfill already guarantees no NULLs remain, so Postgres only verifies rather than rewriting the table.
Step 5 — Cutover code release: deploy code that reads only the new role column.
Step 6 — Drop old column: DROP COLUMN the old representation as the final migration.
Safety invariant: at every point in the chain the schema is a superset of what any deployed code version needs, so a code rollback is just redeploying the previous code with zero database action.
Irreversible step: the final DROP COLUMN in step six is the one step that cannot be undone, which is why it runs last and only once no code version still reads the old column.

Overall recommendation: OIDC federation is the pick whenever the deploy target is a real cloud account that can actually verify identity claims — where it can't, the honest answer flips back to a stored secret.

Long-lived key risk: the long-lived access key pasted into a CI secret sits indefinitely with no forced rotation, and if it leaks (an echoed log line, or a workflow that removed the fork-PR guard) it works from anywhere unconstrained until someone notices and revokes it by hand.

What OIDC removes: instead of a static secret, each CI run presents a short-lived identity token asserting concrete claims (repo, branch, workflow), the cloud role trusts those claims directly, no long-lived token sits in GitHub, and the returned credential is scoped to that one job and expires with it.

Setup requirement: the workflow must explicitly declare permissions: id-token: write, and the cloud side must pin trust to one specific role — without that permission line, federated auth fails; this is least privilege configured on both ends, not a flip-a-switch change.

Fork-PR angle: GitHub Actions withholds secrets from fork PRs by default, but some workflows remove that guard for convenience, opening a path for fork code to read a real secret — with OIDC there is no static secret to leak, shrinking that attack class.
Where OIDC doesn't apply: a plain VPS reached over SSH has no federation relying party at all — no OIDC provider on the VPS side accepting a claim from GitHub.
Correct fallback for VPS: for that target a stored SSH private key is still the correct call, provided it follows real hygiene — never echoed or logged, always masked by GitHub in output.
Safe rotation order: rotate by adding the new public key to the server first and removing the old one only after — never the reverse, or you lock yourself out mid-rotation.
There is no single "always right" base image — the trade-off axis is size/attack-surface versus operability/debuggability, and the right call depends on the environment.
Alpine (~5 MB) is the smallest option but runs on musl libc, not glibc, which sets up a compatibility trap for native dependencies.

A native dependency like bcrypt/sharp compiled on a glibc host and then copied straight into an Alpine runtime will ABI-mismatch and crash on its very first call — a silent runtime crash, not a build-time error.

The fix is building the native dependency inside the very Alpine stage that will run it, never cross-compiling from the host and copying the artifact over — which is exactly why "build inside the same Linux flavor you ship" matters, since the build environment's libc has to match the runtime environment's libc.

Distroless (~20 MB) strips shell, package manager, and every OS utility for the smallest possible attack surface — since anyone who lands inside the container has no tooling to escalate with — but that same absence means you cannot `docker exec ... sh` to debug directly, so debugging shifts to an ephemeral debug container or sidecar.
Debian slim (~70 MB) has full glibc so every native module works with no ABI worry, and a real shell for easy interactive debugging, in exchange for being heavier and carrying a wider CVE surface.

The coherent recommendation is context-conditional — distroless for security-sensitive production, Debian slim (or Alpine if native dependencies are light) for staging, never just "always pick the smallest."

Whichever image is picked should be pinned to an exact version or digest instead of a floating tag like `node:20`, since a floating tag is a moving target that breaks reproducing the exact same image across CI runs months apart.
A flag canary and an infra canary canary completely different axes, so they are complementary mechanisms, not two names for the same idea.

A flag canary keeps ONE code version everywhere and varies which BEHAVIOR a user sees via `isEnabled(flag, userId)` inside already-running code, so rollback is just flipping the flag off, picked up by every instance on its next poll within seconds with no redeploy or infra touched.

An infra canary keeps the code fixed per instance and instead varies which IMAGE VERSION a slice of traffic hits at the load-balancer/proxy layer, so rollback means re-weighting traffic back to the stable image or killing the canary instances, which is slower.

An infra canary is the only mechanism that can revert a regression baked into the image itself, such as a broken dependency bump, a startup crash, or a memory leak — a flag canary cannot catch these because the same broken image runs on every instance regardless of the flag's value.

The two mechanisms also diverge on stickiness: flag rollout hashes the user so one user's experience stays stable across calls, while a raw traffic-weight split happens per request and can flicker the same user between old and new without added session affinity.

A mature team composes both in sequence: first prove the new IMAGE is healthy via an infra canary watching crash rate, latency, and resource usage, then once that image is the stable baseline everywhere, ramp the new FEATURE inside it via a flag from 1% to 10% to 50% to 100%.
Every step of both ramps is gated on metrics, with a kill switch as the universal abort path at any stage on either axis.

A container that builds cleanly, boots cleanly, and serves every GET request while failing only on the first write points to a filesystem-ownership problem inside the image rather than a bug in application logic or a missing directory.

Every `COPY --from=<stage>` instruction in a Dockerfile runs while the build is still executing as root, so any files or directories copied in are owned by root regardless of where a later `USER` instruction appears in the stage.

The `USER` instruction only changes which UID runs the process from that line onward; it does not retroactively change ownership of files or directories that were copied or created earlier in the same build stage.

Reads succeed under a non-root UID because root-owned files and directories grant read and execute permission to "other" by default, so listing or executing them does not require the process to own them.

A write such as `mkdir` or `writeFile` requires write permission on the containing directory, and a root-owned directory with default permissions does not grant that to a non-root UID — which is why the failure surfaces as `EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/reports'` on the first write and not on any read that came before it.

Adding `--chown=1001:1001` to the relevant `COPY --from` instruction, or explicitly creating and `chown`-ing a dedicated writable directory before the `USER` instruction, hands ownership of only the path that needs to be writable to the runtime UID while leaving the rest of the image root-owned.

Running the container as `USER 1001` instead of root exists as a security boundary: a compromised non-root process is limited to whatever paths it owns, whereas a compromised root process could own and modify the entire container filesystem — so removing the `USER` instruction to work around the permission error would eliminate that protection rather than fix the underlying ownership mismatch.

Because a distroless image has no shell to inspect ownership with `stat` or `ls`, verifying the fix requires either overriding the entrypoint to run the image's own `node` binary and call `fs.statSync` on the target directory, or exercising the write endpoint end-to-end after rebuilding and confirming it no longer throws `EACCES`.

Postgres refuses to run `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` inside a transaction block, because the concurrent build needs several independent internal transactions to perform its two-pass scan without holding one long-lived lock — and migration runners such as TypeORM wrap every migration's `up()` in a single transaction by default, which is exactly why the very first deploy attempt fails instantly with that error.

The fix for that first failure is to opt the migration out of the runner's default transaction wrapper (for example setting `transaction = false as const` on the TypeORM migration class), not to retry the same statement as-is.

Disabling the transaction wrapper also strips away the runner's automatic rollback-on-failure safety net for that specific migration, so if the build is interrupted afterward nothing automatically cleans it up.

When a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` build is interrupted mid-way — a deploy timeout, a killed DB connection — Postgres does not roll it back; it leaves the index's catalog entry behind marked invalid, reflected as `pg_index.indisvalid = false`.

An invalid leftover index occupies its name and consumes disk space but is completely ignored by the query planner, which is why the target query is still just as slow even though an index with that name already exists in the catalog.

That same invalid leftover is also why a plain retry of `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_user_email` fails with "relation already exists" — the name is already taken by the broken entry, and issuing the same create statement again cannot repair or replace it.

The correct recovery procedure is to first confirm the index is actually invalid by checking `pg_index.indisvalid` rather than assuming, then drop it (`DROP INDEX`, or `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` to avoid taking a blocking lock during the drop itself), and only then re-run `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` with the transaction wrapper still disabled.

Verification has to go beyond a successful CLI exit code: re-checking `indisvalid = true` after the rebuild and running `EXPLAIN` on the target query confirms the planner is genuinely using the new index, since `CONCURRENTLY` trades a slower two-pass build and no transactional safety net for keeping reads and writes uninterrupted during the build, and that invalid-on-interrupt failure mode needs to be a documented recovery step rather than something the team rediscovers during an incident.

A `deploy` job with no `needs: [lint, test]` and no `if:` condition runs in parallel with the `test` job on every trigger, including pushes on a PR branch — a failing test does nothing to stop it because no dependency links the two jobs.

Adding `needs: [lint, test]` together with `if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` is what turns tests merely passing into tests being required before deploy runs, and it also keeps PR branches from ever triggering a deploy at all.

Explicitly echoing a secret's value (`echo ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}`) can still leak it into the run log, because GitHub's log masking only redacts output that matches the secret's own literal characters — an intentional echo of the value defeats that protection rather than being caught by it.

The exposure from printing a secret in a log is worse on a workflow that can run against fork pull requests, since the trust boundary for who can trigger the job and see its output is different there.
A secret should be referenced only inside a step's `env:` or `with:` block and passed to the tool that needs it directly, never written out through a `run:` shell command.

Caching `node_modules` directly instead of the package manager's own store (such as `~/.npm`) means that on a cache hit, `npm ci` never gets the chance to re-verify the installed tree against `package-lock.json`, so a stale or corrupted cache entry can be silently reused.

Caching the package manager's store keyed on the lockfile hash while still running `npm ci` on every job keeps both properties intact: the store makes the install fast, and the install step itself is what re-verifies integrity against the lockfile.

Pushing every image as `:latest` leaves production pointing at a moving target with no commit-SHA-pinned reference to roll back to; tagging the image with `${{ github.sha }}` and retaining previous tags gives rollback a concrete target to point at.

A senior-style PR review orders findings by blast radius rather than by the order they appear in the file, and separates must-fix-before-merge issues (an ungated deploy path, a leaked secret) from lower-severity mechanical nits (cache correctness, tag mutability).

Proving a new deploy gate actually works means pushing a commit with an intentionally failing test and confirming the Actions run shows `deploy` skipped by `needs:` and never starting — not started-then-failed, which would indicate the gate isn't wired correctly.
